lessons.title: Indexing and length
lessons.recap: Module 2 ended with loops: `for` over a `range` or over the characters of a string, `while`, `break` and `continue`. You have used strings since Module 1, but only as whole values.
lessons.what: A string is a row of characters. Each character has a position number called its **index**, and the first index is 0. `len(text)` tells you how many characters there are.
lessons.why:
Real text has structure: the first letter of a name, the last character of a product code, the length of a password. To use that structure you need to reach single characters.

```python
name = "grace"
print(name[0])      # g   the initial
print(len(name))    # 5
```
lessons.syntax:
```python
text = "Perth"
len(text)    # 5     how many characters
text[0]      # "P"   the first character
text[4]      # "h"   the last one: the biggest index is len(text) - 1
text[-1]     # "h"   negative indexes count back from the end
text[-2]     # "t"
```

```
 P   e   r   t   h
 0   1   2   3   4
-5  -4  -3  -2  -1
```

Strings cannot be changed in place. They are **immutable**. You can read `text[0]`, but you cannot assign to it. To change a string you build a new one.

examples.title: Reading single characters
examples.code:
code = "AB-1042"
print(len(code))
print(code[0])
print(code[2])
print(code[-1])
examples.explain:
- The dash counts as a character, so the length is 7.
- `code[2]` is the third character, because counting starts at 0.
- `code[-1]` is the last character. It saves you writing `code[len(code) - 1]`.

examples.title: Initials
examples.code:
first = "grace"
last = "hopper"
initials = first[0] + last[0]
print(initials)
print(last[len(last) - 1])
examples.explain:
- `first[0]` and `last[0]` are each a one-character string, so `+` joins them.
- The last line reaches the final character the long way: the length is 6, so the last index is 5.

examples.title: Every index with range(len())
examples.explain:
- `len(word)` is 3, so `range(3)` gives 0, 1, 2. Those are exactly the valid indexes.
- Use this form when you need the position as well as the character.

mistakes.title: An index past the end
mistakes.fix: `"cat"` has indexes 0, 1 and 2. Index 3 does not exist. `IndexError` means the position is outside the string. The usual cause is forgetting that the last index is `len(text) - 1`.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(word[3])
          ~~~~^^^
IndexError: string index out of range

mistakes.title: Indexing an empty string
mistakes.fix: An empty string has no characters, so even `[0]` is out of range. This happens with real input: a user presses Enter without typing. Check `len(name) > 0` before you index.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(name[0])
          ~~~~^^^
IndexError: string index out of range

mistakes.title: Trying to change one character
mistakes.fix: Strings are immutable. Build a new string: `word = "b" + word[1]` + the rest. The next lesson (slicing) makes this easy.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    word[0] = "b"
    ~~~~^^^
TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment

lessons.remember: First is [0]. Last is [-1]. The biggest index is len - 1.

quick_checks.explain: `s[1]` is the second character. `s[-2]` is the second from the end, which is the second `l`. The length is 5.

reference.example:

    print(i, word[i])

A user called `J` reports that the program tells them `No name`.

exercises.title: Explain the mirror check
exercises.prompt: Read the code. In your own words, explain what it does, why each step is there, and what it prints. Mention any edge cases you can see.
exercises.model_explanation:
The program checks whether a word reads the same forwards and backwards (a palindrome).

The loop visits every index `i`. `word[i]` is the character counted from the front. `word[-1 - i]` is the matching character counted from the back: when `i` is 0 it is `word[-1]`, when `i` is 1 it is `word[-2]`, and so on. If any pair differs, the flag `same` is set to `False`.

For `level` every pair matches (`l` and `l`, `e` and `e`, `v` and `v`), so it prints `True`.

Edge cases: for an empty string the loop never runs and it prints `True`. A single character also gives `True`. The loop checks each pair twice, which is wasteful but not wrong.
checklist: Said it compares each character with its mirror from the other end
Explained what word[-1 - i] means
Gave the output: True
Mentioned an edge case such as an empty or one-character word

exercises.title: Middle of a word
exercises.prompt:
Read a word with at least one character. If its length is odd, print the middle character. If its length is even, print the two middle characters.

Examples: `cat` gives `a`. `boat` gives `oa`.
hints: `len(word) // 2` is the middle index for an odd length. Try it with `cat`.
For an even length, the two middle characters are at `mid - 1` and `mid`.
exercises.solution_explanation: Whole division by 2 gives the middle index when the length is odd: for `cat`, 3 // 2 is 1. For an even length there is no single middle, so the two characters either side of the halfway point are joined.

exercises.title: Matching positions with two bugs
exercises.prompt:
This program reads two words of the same length. It should count the positions where both words have the same character.

For `cart` and `card` the answer is `3` (c, a and r match). The program prints `1`. It has **two** bugs.
exercises.starter_code:
a = input()
b = input()
count = 0
for i in range(1, len(a)):
    if a[i] == b[i]:
        count = 1
print(count)
hints: Which index does the loop look at first? Which index should it start from?
Look at what happens to `count` on a match. Is it counting?
exercises.solution:
a = input()
b = input()
count = 0
for i in range(len(a)):
    if a[i] == b[i]:
        count += 1
print(count)
exercises.solution_explanation: Bug 1: `range(1, len(a))` skipped index 0, so the first characters were never compared. Bug 2: `count = 1` set the counter to 1 on every match. It should add 1 with `+=`.

lessons.title: Slicing
lessons.recap: Last lesson: `text[i]` reads one character, indexes start at 0, `text[-1]` is the last character, and `len(text)` is the length.
lessons.what: A **slice** is a piece of a string. `text[start:stop]` gives the characters from index `start` up to, but not including, index `stop`.
lessons.why:
Fixed-format text is everywhere: dates, phone numbers, product codes. Slicing pulls out a part in one step. Without it you would join characters one at a time.

Before:

```python
year = date[0] + date[1] + date[2] + date[3]
```

After:

```python
year = date[0:4]
```
lessons.syntax:
```python
text = "2026-11-12"
text[0:4]     # "2026"    from index 0 up to, not including, 4
text[:4]      # "2026"    leave out start: from the beginning
text[5:]      # "11-12"   leave out stop: to the end
text[-2:]     # "12"      the last two characters
text[:-3]     # "2026-11" everything except the last three
text[::2]     # every second character
text[::-1]    # the whole string reversed
```

- It works like `range(start, stop)`: start is included, stop is not.
- The length of `text[a:b]` is `b - a`.
- A slice never raises an `IndexError`. If the numbers run past the end, you get whatever is there, possibly an empty string.

examples.title: Parts of a date
examples.code:
date = "2026-11-12"
year = date[0:4]
month = date[5:7]
day = date[8:]
print(day, month, year)
examples.explain:
- Indexes 0 to 3 hold the year. The slice stops before index 4, which is the first dash.
- `date[5:7]` takes indexes 5 and 6.
- `date[8:]` takes everything from index 8 to the end.

examples.title: From the start, from the end
examples.code:
filename = "report_final.csv"
print(filename[:6])
print(filename[-4:])
print(filename[:-4])
examples.explain:
- `[:6]` is the first six characters.
- `[-4:]` is the last four: a handy way to read a file extension.
- `[:-4]` is everything except the last four: the name without the extension.

examples.title: Steps and reversing
examples.code:
code = "A1B2C3"
print(code[::2])
print(code[1::2])
print(code[::-1])
examples.explain:
- A third number is the step, as in `range`. `[::2]` takes indexes 0, 2, 4.
- `[1::2]` starts at index 1 and takes every second character.
- A step of -1 walks backwards, which reverses the string.

examples.title: Slices are forgiving
examples.code:
word = "cat"
print(word[1:100])
print(len(word[5:]))
print(word[2:1] == "")
examples.explain:
- A stop far past the end simply stops at the end.
- A start past the end gives an empty string, not an error.
- That is different from `word[5]`, which would raise an `IndexError`.

mistakes.title: Expecting the stop index to be included
mistakes.fix: No error. It prints `1`, not `11`. `[5:6]` holds only index 5. For two characters starting at index 5, the stop is 7: start plus the length you want.

mistakes.title: Slicing a number
mistakes.fix: Only sequences such as strings can be sliced. Here `postcode` is an `int`. "Not subscriptable" means "you cannot use square brackets on this". Convert it first: `str(postcode)[:2]`.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(postcode[:2])
          ~~~~~~~~^^^^
TypeError: 'int' object is not subscriptable

mistakes.title: A comma where the colon should be
mistakes.fix: A slice uses a colon. With a comma, Python thinks you are giving two values as one index.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(date[0, 4])
          ~~~~^^^^^^
TypeError: string indices must be integers, not 'tuple'

lessons.remember: text[start:stop] starts at start and stops just before stop.

quick_checks.explain: `s[1:4]` is indexes 1, 2 and 3. `s[:2]` is the first two characters and `s[-2:]` is the last two, joined together.

month = date[3:5]

exercises.title: Explain the two halves
exercises.prompt: Read the code. In your own words, explain what it does, why each step is there, and what it prints. Mention any edge cases you can see.
exercises.starter_code:
word = "racecar"
half = len(word) // 2
left = word[:half]
right = word[-half:]
print(left, right, left == right[::-1])
exercises.model_explanation:
The program splits a word into its first half and last half, then checks whether one is the mirror of the other.

The length is 7, so `half` is 3. `word[:3]` is `rac`. `word[-3:]` is the last three characters, `car`. `right[::-1]` reverses `car` into `rac`, which equals `left`.

It prints `rac car True`. The middle letter `e` is in neither half, which is fine for a palindrome check.

Edge case: for a one-character word, `half` is 0. `word[:0]` is empty, but `word[-0:]` is the same as `word[0:]`, the whole word, because -0 is just 0. So the check would wrongly print `False`.
checklist: Worked out that half is 3
Said left is the first three characters and right is the last three
Gave the output: rac car True
Mentioned an edge case, such as the middle letter being skipped or the -0 problem for short words

lessons.title: Case and cleaning: lower, upper, strip
lessons.recap: Last lesson: `text[start:stop]` takes a slice. The start is included, the stop is not, and a slice never raises an error.
lessons.what: A **method** is a function that belongs to a value. You call it with a dot: `text.lower()`. This lesson covers the methods that change case and the ones that remove unwanted spaces from the ends of a string.
lessons.why:
People type messily: `" Mia_K "`, `"YES"`, `"perth"`. To a computer, `"yes"` and `"YES "` are different strings. Cleaning the text first makes comparisons work.

Before:

```python
if answer == "yes":          # fails for "YES", "Yes " and " yes"
```

After:

```python
if answer.strip().lower() == "yes":
```
lessons.syntax:
```python
text.lower()       # all lowercase
text.upper()       # ALL CAPITALS
text.title()       # First Letter Of Each Word
text.strip()       # remove spaces, tabs and new lines from both ends
text.lstrip()      # left end only
text.rstrip()      # right end only
text.strip("$-")   # remove these characters from both ends
```

- Every one of these **returns a new string**. The original is not changed, because strings are immutable. Store the result: `text = text.strip()`.
- Methods can be chained. They run left to right: `text.strip().lower()`.
- `strip` only works on the ends. Spaces in the middle stay.

examples.title: Compare without caring about case
examples.code:
answer = "YES"
if answer.lower() == "yes":
    print("Confirmed")
print(answer)
examples.explain:
- `answer.lower()` makes a lowercase copy, `"yes"`, just for the comparison.
- The last line shows that `answer` itself still holds `"YES"`.

examples.title: Strip a messy username
examples.code:
raw = "   mia_k  "
clean = raw.strip()
print("[" + raw + "]")
print("[" + clean + "]")
print(len(raw), len(clean))
examples.explain:
- Printing inside square brackets makes invisible spaces visible. It is a useful debugging trick.
- `strip()` removed three spaces from the front and two from the back.

examples.title: Chaining methods
examples.code:
name = "  aDA lovelace "
print(name.strip().title())
print(name.strip().upper())
examples.explain:
- `name.strip()` runs first and gives `"aDA lovelace"`. Then `.title()` runs on that result.
- `title()` capitalises the first letter of each word and lowers the rest.

examples.title: Stripping other characters
examples.code:
price = "$45.00"
print(price.lstrip("$"))
code = "--A17--"
print(code.strip("-"))
print("[" + " a b ".strip() + "]")
examples.explain:
- Give `strip` a string of characters and it removes those from the ends.
- The last line shows the space in the middle is untouched. Only the ends are cleaned.

mistakes.title: Calling the method and throwing the result away
mistakes.fix: No error. It prints `[  mia ]`, spaces and all. `name.strip()` made a clean copy, and then nothing kept it. Write `name = name.strip()`.

mistakes.title: Leaving off the brackets
mistakes.fix: No error. It prints something like `<built-in method upper of str object at 0x...>`. Without `()` you are naming the method, not calling it. Write `name.upper()`.

mistakes.title: Using a string method on a number
mistakes.fix: `AttributeError` means "this type of value does not have that method". `upper` belongs to strings, and `n` is an `int`. Convert first with `str(n)` if you really need text.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(n.upper())
          ^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'upper'

lessons.remember: String methods hand back a new string. Store it or use it straight away.

t = s.strip().lower()
print(t)
print(len(s) - len(t))
quick_checks.explain: `strip()` removes two spaces from each end, then `lower()` changes the case. Four characters were removed in total. The space in the middle is kept.

exercises.title: Explain the city tidy-up
exercises.prompt: Read the code. In your own words, explain what it does, why each step is there, and what it prints. Mention any edge cases you can see.
exercises.starter_code:
raw = "  PERTH, wa "
city = raw.strip()
city = city[:5].title() + city[5:].upper()
print("[" + city + "]")
exercises.model_explanation:
The program tidies a city and state typed in the wrong case.

`raw.strip()` removes the spaces at both ends, leaving `PERTH, wa`. The comma and the space in the middle stay, because `strip` only touches the ends.

Line 3 cuts the text in two. `city[:5]` is `PERTH`, and `.title()` turns it into `Perth`. `city[5:]` is `, wa`, and `.upper()` turns it into `, WA`. Joined, that is `Perth, WA`.

It prints `[Perth, WA]`. The brackets prove there are no stray spaces left.

Edge case: the number 5 is hard-coded. It only works because Perth has five letters. For `SYDNEY, nsw` the cut would land in the wrong place.

lessons.title: Searching: in, find, startswith, endswith, count
lessons.recap: Last lesson: string methods such as `lower()`, `upper()`, `title()` and `strip()` return a new, cleaned-up string. Clean first, then compare.
lessons.what: These tools answer questions about what is inside a string: is this text in there (`in`), where is it (`find`), does the string start or end with it (`startswith`, `endswith`), and how many times does it appear (`count`).
lessons.why:
Log lines, file names and email addresses carry meaning in small markers: the word `ERROR`, the ending `.csv`, the `@` sign. Searching lets you react to those markers without checking characters one at a time.

```python
if "ERROR" in line:
    print("Problem found")
```
lessons.syntax:
```python
"needle" in text           # True or False
"needle" not in text       # the opposite
text.find("needle")        # index where it first starts, or -1 if it is not there
text.startswith("ERR")     # True or False
text.endswith(".csv")      # True or False
text.count("a")            # how many times it appears
```

- All of these are case-sensitive. Use `text.lower()` first when case should not matter.
- `find` gives an index you can use in a slice. Always think about the `-1` case.
- The text you look for is called a **substring**. It can be one character or many.

examples.title: Is it in there?
examples.code:
line = "2026-11-12 ERROR disk full"
print("ERROR" in line)
print("error" in line)
print("error" in line.lower())
examples.explain:
- `in` gives a boolean, so it fits straight into an `if`.
- The second line is `False` because the search is case-sensitive.
- Lowering the line first makes the search ignore case.

examples.title: Find a marker, then slice around it
examples.code:
email = "mia@example.com"
at = email.find("@")
print(at)
print(email[:at])
print(email[at + 1:])
print(email.find("#"))
examples.explain:
- `find` returns 3, the index of the `@`.
- `email[:at]` is everything before it. `email[at + 1:]` is everything after it. The `+ 1` skips the `@` itself.
- When the substring is missing, `find` returns `-1`. It does not raise an error.

examples.title: Starts, ends and counts
examples.code:
filename = "sales_2026.csv"
print(filename.startswith("sales"))
print(filename.endswith(".csv"))
print(filename.count("s"))
print("banana".count("an"))
examples.explain:
- `startswith` and `endswith` are clearer and safer than slicing and comparing.
- `count` works with longer substrings too. `an` appears twice in `banana`.

mistakes.title: Using the result of find without checking for -1
mistakes.fix: No error, which is the danger. There is no `@`, so `at` is -1, and `email[:-1]` means "everything except the last character". It prints `mia.example.co`. Check first: `if at == -1:`.

mistakes.title: Treating find as a yes or no answer
mistakes.fix: No error. It prints `no x`, although the code starts with `x`. `find` returned 0, the index of the match, and 0 counts as false in an `if`. Worse, a missing substring gives -1, which counts as true. For yes or no questions use `in`: `if "x" in code:`.

mistakes.title: Searching for a number inside text
mistakes.fix: `in` on a string needs a string on the left. Put the digit in quotes: `"5" in "12345"`.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 1, in <module>
    print(5 in "12345")
          ^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'in <string>' requires string as left operand, not int

lessons.remember: in answers yes or no. find answers where, and -1 means nowhere.

quick_checks.code:

print(s.find("o"), s.count("o"))
print("wor" in s, s.find("z"))
quick_checks.explain: The first `o` is at index 4, and there are two in total. `wor` is inside `world`. There is no `z`, so `find` gives -1.

lessons.title: Replacing text
lessons.recap: Last lesson: `in` for yes or no, `find` for a position (or -1), `startswith`, `endswith` and `count`.
lessons.what: `text.replace(old, new)` returns a copy of the string in which every occurrence of `old` has been swapped for `new`.
lessons.why:
A lot of cleaning is swapping or deleting characters: remove the spaces from a phone number, turn commas into dots, drop a currency symbol. `replace` does each of these in one call.

Before, you would loop over every character and rebuild the string. After:

```python
digits = phone.replace(" ", "")
```
lessons.syntax:
```python
text.replace("old", "new")       # swap every "old" for "new"
text.replace(" ", "")            # replacing with "" deletes
text.replace("-", "/", 1)        # a third value limits how many are replaced
text.replace("a", "b").replace("c", "d")   # chain several
```

- It replaces **every** match, not just the first.
- It is case-sensitive.
- It returns a new string. Store the result.

examples.title: Delete or swap a character

- With a third value of 1, only the first semicolon is replaced.
- The last line chains two replaces. The first removes the dollar sign, and the second runs on that result and removes the comma. Now the text can go into `float()`.

- Lowering first lets all three match, but the result is then all lowercase too.

lessons.title: split and join
lessons.recap: Last lesson: `text.replace(old, new)` swaps every match and returns a new string. Replacing with `""` deletes.
lessons.what:
`split` cuts a string into pieces wherever a separator appears. `join` does the reverse: it glues pieces together with a separator between them.

The pieces come back as a **list**: several values kept in order under one name. Lists get their own module (Module 4). For now you need three things only: `parts[0]` reads a piece by index, `len(parts)` counts the pieces, and `for p in parts:` loops over them. They work just as they do on strings.
lessons.why:
Most data arrives as lines with separators: `1042,Flat white,4.50`. Finding each comma with `find` and slicing between them is slow and easy to get wrong. `split` does it in one step.

Before:

```python
comma = row.find(",")
first = row[:comma]
```

After:

```python
parts = row.split(",")
first = parts[0]
```
lessons.syntax:
```python
parts = line.split(",")    # cut at every comma
parts[0]                   # the first piece (a string)
parts[-1]                  # the last piece
len(parts)                 # how many pieces
for p in parts:            # each piece in turn

line.split()               # no separator: cut at any run of spaces, ignore the ends
line.split(",", 1)         # cut at the first comma only: at most 2 pieces
"-".join(parts)            # glue the pieces together with "-" between them
```

- Every piece is a string, even if it looks like a number. Convert with `int()` or `float()`.
- The pieces keep any spaces around them. Clean each one with `strip()`.
- `join` is called on the **separator**, and the pieces go inside the brackets.

examples.title: A comma-separated row
examples.code:
row = "1042,Flat white,4.50"
parts = row.split(",")
print(parts)
print(parts[1])
print(len(parts))
print(float(parts[2]) * 2)
examples.explain:
- Printing a list shows its items in square brackets. The quotes tell you each item is a string.
- `parts[1]` is the second piece. Indexes start at 0, as with strings.
- The price is the text `'4.50'` until `float()` converts it.

examples.title: split() with nothing in the brackets
examples.code:
text = "  the   quick fox "
words = text.split()
print(words)
print(len(words))
print(text.split(" "))
examples.explain:
- With no separator, `split()` treats any run of spaces as one gap and ignores spaces at the ends. This is the one to use for words.
- `split(" ")` cuts at every single space, so extra spaces produce empty strings. That is rarely what you want.

examples.title: Loop over the pieces
examples.explain:
- The loop gives one piece per round.
- Without `strip()` the second piece would be `" bread "`, with a space on each side.

examples.title: Glue pieces back together
examples.code:

parts = date.split("/")
print("-".join(parts))
print(" ".join("a  b   c".split()))
examples.explain:
- `"-".join(parts)` puts a dash between the pieces, and none at the ends.
- The last line is a common trick: split into words, then join with single spaces. It tidies any amount of spacing.

mistakes.title: Asking for a piece that is not there
mistakes.fix: The row has only two pieces, at indexes 0 and 1. Note the message says **list** index this time. Real data often has short rows, so check `len(parts)` before you index.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 3, in <module>

          ~~~~~^^^
IndexError: list index out of range

mistakes.title: Forgetting that the pieces are strings
mistakes.fix: No error. It prints `34`. The pieces are `'3'` and `'4'`, so `+` joins them. Convert each one: `int(parts[0]) + int(parts[1])`.

mistakes.title: join the wrong way round

lessons.remember: split: one string into pieces. join: pieces into one string, written separator.join(pieces).

lessons.title: Looping over strings
lessons.recap: Last lesson: `split` cuts a string into a list of pieces, and `sep.join(pieces)` glues them back together. On the list you can use `parts[0]`, `len(parts)` and a `for` loop.
lessons.what: A `for` loop can walk through a string one character at a time. This lesson is about the patterns that sit on top of that loop: counting, searching, checking each character against a set, and comparing neighbours.
lessons.why:
Methods such as `count` and `replace` handle the common cases. But many questions are too specific for a method: how many characters are digits, where is the first capital, are any two neighbours the same. For those you look at each character yourself.

```python
digits = 0
for ch in text:
    if ch in "0123456789":
        digits += 1
```
lessons.syntax:
```python
for ch in text:                 # each character, when the position does not matter
for i in range(len(text)):      # each index, when you need the position
    text[i]                     #   the character there
    text[i + 1]                 #   its right-hand neighbour (careful at the end)

if ch in "aeiou":               # is this character one of these?
```

- `ch in "aeiou"` replaces a long chain of `ch == "a" or ch == "e" or ...`.
- To compare each character with the next one, stop one early: `range(len(text) - 1)`.

lessons.title: Building strings
lessons.recap: Last lesson: looping over characters with `for ch in text`, over positions with `range(len(text))`, and testing a character with `ch in "..."`.
lessons.what: Because strings cannot be changed in place, you make a changed version by **building** a new string: start with an empty string and add pieces to it, usually inside a loop. The `*` operator repeats a string.
lessons.why:
Removing the vowels, reversing a word, keeping only the digits: each of these produces new text from old. The pattern is the accumulator you already use for totals, but with text.

```python
total = 0            result = ""
for n in ...:        for ch in ...:
    total += n           result += ch
```
lessons.syntax:
```python
result = ""              # 1. start empty
for ch in text:
    if keep(ch):         # 2. decide
        result += ch     # 3. add to the end
result = ch + result     # adding at the FRONT reverses the order

"-" * 10                 # "----------"  repeat a string
"ab" * 3                 # "ababab"
```

- `result += piece` is short for `result = result + piece`.
- Only strings can be added. Convert numbers with `str()` first.

lessons.title: Formatting and alignment
lessons.recap: Last lesson: building a new string piece by piece with `result += piece`, and repeating with `"-" * n`. In Module 1 you met f-strings and `:.2f`.
lessons.what: Inside the braces of an f-string, everything after the colon is a **format spec**: a short code that sets the width, the alignment, the padding and the number of decimal places.
lessons.why:
Reports and receipts need columns that line up. Padding by hand means counting characters and adding spaces. A format spec does the counting.

Before:

```python
print(item + " " * (12 - len(item)) + str(price))
```

After:

```python
print(f"{item:<12}{price:>8.2f}")
```
lessons.syntax:
```python
f"{text:<10}"      # left-aligned in 10 columns (padded with spaces on the right)
f"{text:>10}"      # right-aligned
f"{text:^10}"      # centred
f"{text:.<10}"     # a character before the arrow is used as the padding
f"{num:>8.2f}"     # width 8, right-aligned, 2 decimal places
f"{n:05d}"         # whole number padded with zeros to 5 digits
f"{n:,}"           # thousands separators: 1,234,567
f"{ratio:.1%}"     # as a percentage: 0.256 -> 25.6%
```

- The order inside the spec is: padding character, alignment, width, comma, `.decimals`, type.
- The width is a minimum. Text that is longer is **not** cut off.
- Numbers are right-aligned by default, and text is left-aligned.

- A comma in the spec adds thousands separators.
- `%` multiplies by 100 and adds the percent sign.

lessons.title: Validating text
lessons.recap: Last lesson: format specs inside f-strings, such as `{name:<10}`, `{price:>8.2f}` and `{n:05d}`, for output that lines up.
lessons.what: To **validate** text is to check that it has the shape you expect before you use it. Python strings have methods that answer `True` or `False` about their contents, such as `isdigit()` and `isalpha()`.
lessons.why:
`int("abc")` crashes the program. Real input is full of surprises: empty lines, letters where digits should be, extra spaces. Checking first lets the program give a clear message and carry on.

Before:

```python
age = int(input())           # crashes on "thirty"
```

After:

```python
raw = input().strip()
if raw.isdigit():
    age = int(raw)
else:
    print("Invalid age")
```
lessons.syntax:
```python
text.isdigit()    # every character is a digit 0-9
text.isalpha()    # every character is a letter
text.isalnum()    # every character is a letter or a digit
text.isupper()    # every letter is a capital (and there is at least one letter)
text.islower()    # every letter is lowercase (and there is at least one letter)
text.isspace()    # every character is a space, tab or new line
```

- An **empty string gives `False`** for every one of these.
- `isdigit()` is `False` for `"-5"` and `"4.5"`, because `-` and `.` are not digits.
- These check the whole string. To ask about parts, slice first or loop over the characters: `ch.isdigit()`.
- Combine them with `len()`, `in` and `and` to describe a format.

examples.title: Check, then convert
examples.explain:
- `int(raw)` only runs after `isdigit()` has confirmed it is safe.
- The last line shows three cases that surprise people: a decimal point, a minus sign and an empty string all give `False`.

examples.title: Describe a format with several checks
examples.explain:
- The text is cleaned first. With the spaces still on, `isdigit()` would be `False`.
- Two conditions describe an Australian postcode: exactly four characters, all of them digits.

examples.title: Ask about each character
examples.code:
password = "sunshine7"
has_digit = False
for ch in password:
    if ch.isdigit():
        has_digit = True
print(has_digit)
print(password.isalpha(), password.isalnum())
examples.explain:
- "Contains at least one digit" needs a loop and a flag, because `password.isdigit()` asks whether **all** the characters are digits.
- `isalpha()` is `False` because of the `7`. `isalnum()` is `True`: letters and digits only.

mistakes.title: Checking before cleaning
mistakes.fix: No error. It prints `False`, although a person would call ` 42` a number. The leading space is not a digit. Strip first: `raw.strip().isdigit()`.

mistakes.title: Leaving the brackets off the check
mistakes.fix: No error. It prints `number` for `abc`. Without `()`, `raw.isdigit` is the method itself, and that always counts as true in an `if`. Write `raw.isdigit()`.

mistakes.title: Converting first and checking second
mistakes.fix: The conversion on line 2 crashes before the check on line 3 can run. The check must come first, and the conversion goes inside the `if`.

number = int(raw)
if raw.isdigit():
    print(number)
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    number = int(raw)
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'

lessons.remember: Clean, check, then convert. An empty string fails every is-check.

quick_checks.explain: A space is neither a letter nor a digit, so `"abc 123".isalnum()` is `False`. `isupper()` only looks at the letters: `"A1"` has one letter and it is a capital. `"12"` has no letters at all, so the answer is `False`.

exercises.solution_explanation: The length check comes first in the `and` chain. If it fails, Python does not work out the rest, so `code[3]` is never reached on a short string. The letters need two checks: `isalpha()` rejects `AB1`, and `isupper()` rejects lowercase.

exercises.solution_explanation: Bug 1: `and` made the length test impossible to meet. It must be `or`. Bug 2: `isalpha` without brackets is always true, so `not` made it always false and the rule never fired. Bug 3: `name[0]` crashed on an empty line. Using `elif` means the first character is only read when the length is already known to be at least 3.

exercises.title: Explain the character census

The loop visits the characters one at a time. The `if` / `elif` / `else` chain puts each character in exactly one group: a letter, else a digit, else anything that is left (here, the space).

`Room` and `B` give 5 letters. `1` and `2` give 2 digits. The single space is the 1 other.

It prints `5 2 1`. The three counts always add up to `len(text)`, because every character lands in one branch.

Edge case: for an empty string the loop never runs and it prints `0 0 0`.
checklist: Said each character goes into exactly one of three groups
Said the space is what lands in the else branch

lessons.title: Simple parsing: pulling fields out of a line
lessons.recap: Last lesson: checking text before using it, with `isdigit()`, `isalpha()` and friends, plus `len()` and `and`. Before that: `strip`, `find`, slices, `split`.
lessons.what: **Parsing** means taking a line of text that follows a pattern and pulling out the pieces you need, as values you can work with. A piece is often called a **field**.
lessons.why:
Programs are fed text written for people or for other programs: `timeout = 30`, `2026-11-12 ERROR Disk full`, `2 x Flat white @ $4.50`. Until the line is parsed it is just characters. After parsing you have a name, a number, a date.

This lesson adds no new methods. It is about combining the ones you know in a reliable order. The whole of Module 8 (files) builds on it.
lessons.syntax:
The four-step recipe:

```python
line = line.strip()             # 1. clean the whole line
parts = line.split(",")         # 2. cut it at the separator
name = parts[0].strip()         # 3. pick each field and clean it
qty = int(parts[1])             # 4. convert the ones that are numbers
```

When there is no regular separator, cut around a marker with `find`:

```python
eq = line.find("=")
key = line[:eq].strip()         # everything before the marker
value = line[eq + 1:].strip()   # everything after it
```

- `split(sep, 1)` cuts at the first separator only. Use it when the last field may contain the separator.
- Before `parts[2]`, be sure there are at least 3 parts: check `len(parts)`.

examples.title: A settings line: key = value
examples.code:
line = "  timeout = 30  "
eq = line.find("=")
key = line[:eq].strip()
value = line[eq + 1:].strip()
print(key)
print(int(value) * 2)
examples.explain:
- `find` locates the equals sign. The slices take what is on each side of it.
- Each side is stripped, because there were spaces around the `=`.
- `value` is the text `"30"` until `int()` converts it.

examples.title: A log line with a free-text message
examples.code:
line = "2026-11-12 09:15:02 ERROR Disk full on /dev/sda1"
parts = line.split(" ", 3)
time = parts[1]
hour = int(time.split(":")[0])
print(parts[2])
print(hour)
print(parts[3])
examples.explain:
- `split(" ", 3)` makes at most three cuts, so the message stays whole in `parts[3]`.
- The time is parsed a second time: split at the colons, and the first piece is the hour.
- `int("09")` is 9.

examples.title: The text between two markers
examples.code:
text = "Order [A-1042] shipped"
start = text.find("[")
end = text.find("]")
print(text[start + 1:end])
examples.explain:
- `start + 1` skips the opening bracket itself.
- The slice stops before `end`, so the closing bracket is left out too.

examples.title: A row of mixed fields
examples.code:
row = "Flat white, 2, 4.50"
parts = row.split(",")
name = parts[0].strip()
qty = int(parts[1])
price = float(parts[2])
print(f"{name}: {qty * price:.2f}")
examples.explain:
- This is the full recipe: cut, pick, clean, convert.
- `int(" 2")` and `float(" 4.50")` ignore the spaces, so only the name needs `strip()`.

mistakes.title: Assuming the line has every field
mistakes.fix: The line has no `=`, so `split` gives one piece and index 1 does not exist. Check `len(parts)` first, or check `"=" in line`.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 3, in <module>
    print(parts[1])
          ~~~~~^^^
IndexError: list index out of range

mistakes.title: Converting a field that still has extra text
mistakes.fix: `int()` and `float()` accept spaces around a number, but nothing else. Remove the unit first, for example by splitting at the space and taking the first piece.
mistakes.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(int(field))
          ~~~^^^^^^^
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '12 items'

mistakes.title: Splitting at the wrong separator
mistakes.fix: No error. It prints `1`. The line uses semicolons, so splitting at commas finds nothing and returns the whole line as a single piece. When a parse gives strange results, print `parts` and `len(parts)` first.

lessons.remember: Clean, cut, pick, convert. Count the pieces before you index.

quick_checks.explain: The first field is `id=7`, and splitting it at `=` gives `7` as the second piece. `find("name=")` gives the index where that marker starts. Adding 5, the length of `name=`, moves to just after it.

exercises.solution_explanation: The limit of 1 means only the first equals sign is a cut point, so a value such as `a=b` stays whole. Each piece is stripped separately, which removes the spaces that were next to the `=` as well as those at the ends of the line.

A sensor sends lines like `temp: 21.5C`. This program should print the temperature plus 1, so `22.5` for that line. It crashes:

exercises.title: Explain the messy row
exercises.prompt: Read the code. In your own words, explain what it does, why each step is there, and what it prints. Mention any edge cases you can see.
exercises.starter_code:
row = "  Pen ,3, 1.50 ,  "
parts = row.strip().split(",")
name = parts[0].strip()
qty = int(parts[1])
price = float(parts[2])
print(len(parts), name, qty * price)
exercises.model_explanation:
The program parses a comma-separated row with untidy spacing and a trailing comma.

`row.strip()` removes the spaces at the two ends, leaving `Pen ,3, 1.50 ,`. Splitting at commas gives **four** pieces: `Pen `, `3`, ` 1.50 ` and an empty string, because there is nothing after the last comma.

The name is stripped to `Pen`. `int("3")` is 3. `float(" 1.50 ")` is 1.5: the conversions ignore surrounding spaces, so they need no `strip()`.

It prints `4 Pen 4.5`.

Edge cases: the empty fourth piece is harmless here because it is never used. But an empty quantity, as in `Pen,,1.50`, would make `int("")` raise a `ValueError`.

Explained why there are 4 pieces (the trailing comma)
Gave the output: 4 Pen 4.5
Mentioned that int/float ignore spaces, or what an empty field would do

exercises.title: Receipt line
exercises.prompt:
A till prints lines like this:

```

```

That is a quantity, ` x `, an item name, ` @ $`, and a unit price. Read one such line and print the item and the line total:

```

```

The item name can itself contain ` x `, as in `1 x Box x Large @ $5`. The quantity always ends at the **first** ` x `.
hints: Find the two markers: the first `" x "` and the `" @ $"`.
The quantity is before the first marker. The name is between the markers. The price is after the second one.
Each marker has a length. Skip past it: 3 characters for `" x "`, 4 for `" @ $"`.

line = input()
x = line.find(" x ")
at = line.find(" @ $")
qty = int(line[:x])
name = line[x + 3:at]
price = float(line[at + 4:])
print(f"{name}: ${qty * price:.2f}")
exercises.solution_explanation: `find` returns the first ` x `, so an `x` inside the item name does not confuse it. The three slices take the text before the first marker, between the two markers, and after the second. Adding each marker's length to its index skips over the marker itself.

lessons.title: Strings mixed practice
lessons.recap: This module covered indexing, slicing, case and `strip`, searching, `replace`, `split` and `join`, looping over characters, building strings, format specs, validating, and parsing a line into fields.
lessons.what: There is no new syntax in this lesson. It is a **method** for string problems, which are the most common kind of question in coding assessments: read the examples, clean the input, cut it up, convert, then build the output.
lessons.why:
Knowing each tool is not the same as knowing which one to pick. Under time pressure, people skip the cleaning step, test only the tidy example, and fail on the messy one.

A fixed order of work stops that:

1. **Read** the examples, including the awkward ones. What changes between input and output?
2. **Clean**: `strip()`, and `lower()` if case should not matter.
3. **Cut**: `split`, or `find` and a slice.
4. **Convert**: `int()`, `float()`, after checking if the input may be wrong.
5. **Build** the output: an f-string, `join`, or a loop.
6. **Test the ugly inputs**: empty, one item, extra spaces, wrong case.
lessons.syntax:
Pick the tool by the job:

```python
# One character or a fixed position      text[0]   text[-1]   text[2:5]
# Tidy the ends, ignore case             text.strip().lower()
# Is it there? Where?                    "x" in text     text.find("x")
# Starts or ends with                    text.startswith("a")   text.endswith(".csv")
# Swap or delete characters              text.replace(",", "")
# Fields with a separator                text.split(",")   text.split()   text.split("=", 1)
# Glue pieces together                   "-".join(parts)
# Look at every character                for ch in text:
# Make a changed copy                    result = ""  ...  result += ch
# Is it the right kind of text?          text.isdigit()   text.isalpha()
# Line things up                         f"{name:<10}{price:>8.2f}"
```

examples.title: Clean, cut, re-case, rebuild
examples.code:
raw = "  SMITH,  john "
parts = raw.strip().split(",")
last = parts[0].strip().title()
first = parts[1].strip().title()
print(first + " " + last)
examples.explain:
- Clean: `strip()` on the whole line.
- Cut: split at the comma into the two names.
- Each piece is stripped again, because there were spaces after the comma, and put into title case.
- Build: join them in the new order.

examples.title: Fields inside fields
examples.code:
line = "level=ERROR code=500 path=/api/users"
for field in line.split():
    key = field.split("=")[0]
    value = field.split("=")[1]
    if key == "code":
        print(int(value) >= 500)
print(line.count("="))
examples.explain:
- The outer split cuts the line into three `key=value` fields.
- Each field is then split again at the `=`.
- Only the `code` field is used: its value is converted and compared.
- Parsing is often two levels deep like this.

mistakes.title: Testing only the tidy example
mistakes.fix: No error. It prints `False`. The code works for `a,b` but not for `a, b`, because the second piece is `" b"` with a space. Always try an input with extra spaces. Here the fix is `.strip()` on the piece.

mistakes.title: Comparing before cleaning
mistakes.fix: No error. It prints `unknown`. The comparison happens on the raw text, capitals and spaces included. Clean first: `cmd = cmd.strip().lower()`.

lessons.remember: Clean, cut, convert, build. Then test the ugly inputs.

exercises.prompt:
A tiny chat program understands two commands:

- `quit` or `exit`, in any mix of capitals and with spaces around it: print `Goodbye`
- `say` followed by a space and some text: print that text, without spaces at its ends. The word `say` can be in any case.

exercises.title: Explain two ways of counting
exercises.prompt: Read the code. In your own words, explain what it does, why each step is there, and what it prints. Mention any edge cases you can see.
exercises.model_explanation:
The program counts the error entries in a comma-separated line, in two different ways.

The loop splits the line at the commas and looks at each field. The field is stripped and put into capitals, then compared with `ERROR`. Three fields match: `ERROR`, `error` and ` Error `. So `count` is 3.

The second way puts the whole line into capitals and uses `count("ERROR")`, which counts every place those five letters appear. That is also 3.

It prints `3 3`.

The two methods agree here but they are not the same. The loop only counts fields that are exactly the word. `count` would also count `ERRORS` or `NO_ERROR`, because it finds the letters inside longer text. For data with fields, the loop is the safer one.
checklist: Said the loop compares each cleaned field with ERROR
Said count finds the letters anywhere in the uppercased line
Gave the output: 3 3
Explained when the two methods would give different answers

Read one duration and print the total number of minutes.

Add `number * 60` for `h` and `number` for `m`.

exercises.title: Log summary
exercises.prompt:
Read log lines until a line that says `END`. Each proper line looks like `LEVEL: message`, where the level is `ERROR`, `WARN` or `INFO` in any mix of capitals, possibly with spaces around it.

Count the lines for each level. A line is **skipped** (and counted as skipped) if it has no colon or if its level is not one of the three. Blank lines are skipped too.

Then print four lines:

```
ERROR 2
WARN 1
INFO 0
Skipped 1
```

That example is for these lines: `ERROR: disk full`, `warn: slow reply`, `hello`, ` Error : again`, `END`.
exercises.starter_code: # Read lines until END. Count each level and the skipped lines.

stdin_tests.name: the example
stdin_tests.stdin:
ERROR: disk full
warn: slow reply
hello
 Error : again
END

stdin_tests.name: an unknown level and a blank line
stdin_tests.stdin:
INFO: started
DEBUG: x=1

info: done
END

hints: Use `while True`, and `break` when the line is `END`.
If `":" not in line`, count it as skipped and `continue`.
Otherwise the level is the text before the first colon: split with a limit of 1, strip it, and put it in capitals.
exercises.solution:
errors = 0
warns = 0
infos = 0
skipped = 0
while True:
    line = input()
    if line == "END":
        break
    if ":" not in line:
        skipped += 1
        continue
    level = line.split(":", 1)[0].strip().upper()
    if level == "ERROR":
        errors += 1
    elif level == "WARN":
        warns += 1
    elif level == "INFO":
        infos += 1
    else:
        skipped += 1
print(f"ERROR {errors}")
print(f"WARN {warns}")
print(f"INFO {infos}")
print(f"Skipped {skipped}")
exercises.solution_explanation: The loop reads until `END`. Lines with no colon, which includes blank lines, are skipped straight away. For the rest, the level is whatever comes before the first colon, cleaned with `strip()` and `upper()` so that ` Error ` and `warn` match. Anything that is not one of the three levels is also counted as skipped.
